fields.meta_title: The Priesthood of All Believers: What It Means to Be a Holy Priesthood
fields.description: Scripture calls every believer a holy, royal priesthood. Here is what that means spiritually — set apart, given access to God through Christ — and how to live it out in worship, intercession, and everyday witness.
fields.body_html:
When the New Testament wants to tell ordinary believers who they now are, one of the boldest things it says is this: you are priests. Not that you have a priest, or go to one, but that you are one. “You yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5). It is easy to read past a sentence like that, because for most of us the word “priest” belongs to someone else — a robed professional, a special class. But Peter is writing to fishermen and slaves and housewives, and he means every one of them.

To be a holy priesthood is both a dignity and a calling. Spiritually, it means you have been set apart for God and given a nearness to him that once belonged only to a chosen few. Practically, it means you now have sacrifices to offer, people to carry to God, and a God to make known. Here is what that ancient, thrilling title means — and how to live inside it.

What Scripture actually calls you

The idea did not begin with Peter. At Sinai, before a single sacrifice had been offered, God told a rescued slave-people what he intended them to be: “you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). That was always the goal — a whole people, not a caste, who would belong to God and serve him. Israel’s later priesthood, with its one tribe and its towering high priest, was a temporary arrangement for a people not yet ready; the heart of God was for the whole nation to draw near.

What Sinai promised, the gospel delivers. Peter takes the very words of Exodus and hands them to the church: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). John says the same with wonder in the book of Revelation — Christ “made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father” (Revelation 1:6), and the redeemed sing that he has made them “a kingdom and priests to our God” (Revelation 5:10). This is what the Reformers called the priesthood of all believers: not that ministers are unnecessary, but that no Christian stands at a distance, needing another human being to reach God for them. If you are in Christ, the title is yours.

Holy: set apart before it is spotless

Notice that the priesthood is a holy one — and it helps to know what that word carries. “Holy” means, first of all, set apart, belonging wholly to God. A holy vessel in the temple was not a morally better cup than one at home; it was a cup reserved for God alone. So when Scripture calls you a holy priesthood, its first meaning is not that you have already become spotless, but that you have been claimed. You are God’s own possession, marked off for him, no longer your own.

That reordering matters, because many believers hear “holy” and immediately feel disqualified. But holiness begins as a gift of belonging before it becomes a work of character. Andrew Murray pressed this in Holy in Christ: our holiness is not first something we manufacture but Someone we are joined to — Christ, who is himself our holiness, whose life is meant to work its way out into ours. Being set apart is the root; being made pure is the fruit that grows from it. God does not wait for you to be clean before he claims you; he claims you, and then sets about making you what he has called you.

And so the moral call still comes, warmly and without apology: “as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy’” (1 Peter 1:16). A priest reserved for God lives like it. Hudson Taylor caught the rhythm of it in the title of one of his little books — Separation and Service: separated unto God first, and out of that separation, sent to serve. The two always travel together. You cannot serve as a priest what you have not first been set apart for.

The torn veil: your access to God

Here is the spiritual privilege at the center of it all. Under the old covenant, the way to God was hedged with warnings. Behind a heavy curtain lay the Most Holy Place, where God’s presence dwelt, and only the high priest could enter — once a year, and never without blood. The message was unmistakable: God is holy, and sinners cannot simply stroll into his presence.

Then, at the death of Jesus, that curtain tore from top to bottom. The letter to the Hebrews explains what it means for you: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh… let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:19–22). The way is open. What terrified an entire nation is now the standing invitation of every believer: “let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16).

This is why the priesthood of all believers is such good news. A priest, at bottom, is someone permitted to come near. You do not need another human being to carry your prayers up for you, or to pronounce you accepted, for “there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). He is the great High Priest; through him the smallest, newest believer has an access the holiest Old Testament saint never knew. Frederick Brotherton Meyer traced this whole reality through Hebrews in The Way Into the Holiest — the wonder that the innermost room, once forbidden, is now the believer’s daily home. Do not leave that door standing open and never walk through it.

The sacrifices a priest brings

A priest exists to offer. That is the practical heart of the calling: Peter says you are a holy priesthood precisely so as “to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5). The old sacrifices of bulls and goats are finished, fulfilled once for all in Christ. But the New Testament names a whole new altar-load of offerings that are now yours to bring.

The first sacrifice is yourself. “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1). Not an animal on an altar, but your own body, your own days, laid down alive for God’s use. This is the priest’s foundational act, renewed every morning: here I am; I am yours; use me today.

The second sacrifice is praise. “Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15). Worship is not merely how we feel; it is something we bring — a deliberate offering of thanks and adoration, especially when it costs us, which is why Scripture calls it a sacrifice. And prayer itself rises like the old temple incense before God: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2).

The third sacrifice is a life poured out for others. The same passage goes straight from praise to practical love: “Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God” (Hebrews 13:16). A gift given, a meal cooked, a burden carried, money released to those in need — Paul called one such gift “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). Ordinary kindness, done for God, becomes worship laid on the altar. The priesthood turns the whole of a life into something that can be offered.

A priest stands between: intercession and witness

A priest faces two directions. He comes near to God, yes — but he does so on behalf of others, and then turns back to represent God to them. Your priesthood has both movements, and neither is optional.

Toward God, the priestly work is intercession — carrying other people, by name, into the presence you have been given access to. If every believer is a priest, then every believer has a congregation to pray for: a spouse, a wandering child, a neighbor, a nation. Andrew Murray called this The Ministry of Intercession and grieved that so few Christians take it up, when it is among the highest exercises of the priesthood — standing in the gap, pleading for people who may never pray for themselves. You have been let behind the curtain; do not go in empty-handed. Bring people with you.

Toward the world, the priestly work is witness. Peter says you are a royal priesthood so “that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). The priest represents God to people — makes him known, speaks well of him, shows by a set-apart life that he is worth belonging to. This happens far more often at a kitchen table or a workbench than in a pulpit. Wherever you have been placed, you are God’s representative there, a priest in an apron or a hard hat, letting people see and hear what he is like.

How to live as a priest this week

All of this can stay a lovely idea unless it becomes a handful of habits. So let the truth land in the ordinary week:

  • Draw near, daily. The veil is torn; the throne of grace is open (Hebrews 4:16). Do not let a day pass without walking through the door that cost Christ his life to open. A priest who never enters the presence has forgotten what he is.
  • Offer yourself each morning. Before the day claims you, present your body a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1). Hand him the hours in advance and the whole day becomes an offering.
  • Make ordinary work an offering. “Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Colossians 3:17). The commute, the spreadsheet, the dishes — done for him, they rise as a fragrant sacrifice.
  • Carry others in. Name three people and intercede for them this week. Priesthood means you were let near not only for yourself.
  • Make him known. Speak one true, glad word about God to someone who needs it. You are here to proclaim his excellencies, right where you are.

This is who you are: not a spectator kept at a distance, but a priest with an open way to God, a set of sacrifices to bring, people to carry in your heart, and a Lord to make known. The title was never meant to flatter you; it was meant to send you. So draw near with confidence, offer yourself and your praise and your ordinary faithful days, and go on proclaiming the excellencies of the One who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
